extraction.name: SciQ
extraction.description: SciQ is a dataset of 13,679 multiple choice science exam questions crowdsourced using a two-step process: first, crowd workers select domain-relevant passages and formulate questions; second, another worker selects or writes answer distractors aided by a model trained to predict plausible distractors. The dataset includes a multiple choice version and a direct-answer version.
extraction.creator: Johannes Welbl, Nelson F. Liu, Matt Gardner
extraction.citeAs: Welbl, J., Liu, N. F., & Gardner, M. (2017). Crowdsourcing Multiple Choice Science Questions. arXiv:1707.06209.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: A two-step crowdsourcing process was used. In the first step, crowd workers were shown three filtered textbook paragraphs and asked to choose one and formulate a question answerable from the passage. In the second step, another crowd worker validated the question and selected or wrote answer distractors, aided by model-generated distractor suggestions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: A small percentage of the passages were obtained from unreleasable texts, so the direct answer version of SciQ is slightly smaller, with 10481 questions in train, 887 in dev, and 884 in test.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Science study textbooks from CK-12 and OpenStax, covering biology, chemistry, earth science and physics from elementary to college introductory level. A total of 28 books were compiled.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A rule-based document filter was applied to individual paragraphs of the base corpus. Sentences were filtered out based on lexical, grammatical, pragmatical and complexity-based rules (e.g., questions, exclamations, sentences with no verb phrase, modal verbs, imperative phrases, demonstrative pronouns, personal pronouns other than third-person, sentences beginning with a pronoun, containing first names, having less than 6 or more than 18 tokens, containing special characters, etc.).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Two-step crowdsourcing on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Step 1: Workers chose one of three presented textbook paragraphs and formulated a science exam question with a correct answer (no yes/no questions, 6-30 words, answer up to 3 words, querying general principles). Step 2: A second worker validated the question (marking ungrammatical, false answer, unrelated to science, or requiring very specific knowledge) and selected up to two of six model-suggested distractors and wrote at least one distractor themselves.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: 7.2% of questions were rejected in the second task as failing quality control. In 12.1% of cases in the first task, all three documents were rejected by workers. 36.1% of distractors in the final dataset were generated by the model (workers accepted model suggestions around half the time).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: A total of 175 workers participated in the whole crowdsourcing project. Workers were required to have Amazon Mechanical Turk Master's status.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A random forest distractor ranking model trained on 3705 science exam questions, using GloVe embeddings, WordNet, OpenIE triples from Simple Wikipedia, and scikit-learn's random forest implementation.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Neural models do not beat simple information retrieval baselines on the multiple choice version of this dataset. A small percentage of passages were obtained from unreleasable texts, making the direct answer version smaller. The distractor model quality is not high enough to use predictions directly without additional filtering by crowd workers.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing for science exam question answering systems; studying neural reading comprehension models in medium-data settings; augmenting training data for answering real science exam questions.

name.evidence: With a total budget of $10,415, we collected 13,679 multiple choice science questions, which we call SciQ.

description.evidence: With a total budget of $10,415, we collected 13,679 multiple choice science questions, which we call SciQ. This dataset has a multiple choice version, where the task is to select the correct answer using whatever background information a system can find given a question and several answer options, and a direct answer version, where given a passage and a question a system must predict the span within the passage that answers the question.

inLanguage.evidence: We present a novel method for obtaining high-quality, domain-targeted multiple choice questions from crowd workers.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: The method is a two-step process: first we present a set of candidate passages to a crowd worker, letting the worker choose one of the passages and ask a question about it. Second, another worker takes the question and answer generated in the first step and produces three distractors, aided by a model trained to predict good answer distractors.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: The task was advertised on Amazon Mechanical Turk, requiring Master's status for the crowdworkers... we support the process in our crowdsourcing task with model-generated answer distractor suggestions.

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: A small percentage of the passages were obtained from unreleasable texts, so the direct answer version of SciQ is slightly smaller, with 10481 questions in train, 887 in dev, and 884 in test.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: We chose science study textbooks as our base corpus because they are directly relevant and linguistically tailored towards a student audience... we compiled a list of 28 books from various online learning resources, including CK-12 and OpenStax, who share this material under a Creative Commons License. The books are about biology, chemistry, earth science and physics and span elementary level to college introductory material.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: We designed a rule-based document filter model into which individual paragraphs of the base corpus are fed. The system classifies individual sentences and accepts a paragraph if a minimum number of sentences is accepted... Specifically, sentences were filtered out if they i) were a question or exclamation ii) had no verb phrase iii) contained modal verbs iv) contained imperative phrases v) contained demonstrative pronouns vi) contained personal pronouns other than third-person vii) began with a pronoun viii) contained first names ix) had less than 6 or more than 18 tokens or more than 2 commas x) contained special characters other than punctuation xi) had more than three tokens beginning uppercase xii) mentioned a graph, table or web link xiii) began with a discourse marker xiv) contained absolute wording xv) contained instructional vocabulary.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: The task was advertised on Amazon Mechanical Turk, requiring Master's status for the crowdworkers, and paying a compensation of 0.30$ per HIT... The first instruction was to judge whether the question could appear in a school science exam; questions could be marked as ungrammatical, having a false answer, being unrelated to science or requiring very specific background knowledge. The second instruction was to select up to two of the six suggested distractors, and to write at least one distractor by themselves such that there is a total of three.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: The task was advertised on Amazon Mechanical Turk, requiring Master's status for the crowdworkers, and paying a compensation of 0.30$ per HIT.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: The total proportion of questions passing was 92.8%... In 12.1% of the cases all three documents were rejected... On average, crowd workers found the predicted distractors good enough to include in the final question around half of the time, resulting in 36.1% of the distractors in the final dataset being generated by the model.

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: A total of 175 workers participated in the whole crowdsourcing project... requiring Master's status for the crowdworkers

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: For classification, we train r on actual in-domain questions with observed false answers as the plausible (good) distractors... As classifier we chose a random forest (Breiman, 2001)... We used scikit-learn's implementation of random forests with default parameters. We used 500 trees and enforced at least 4 samples per tree leaf.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: neural models do not beat simple information retrieval baselines on the multiple choice version of this dataset, leaving room for research on applying neural models in settings where training examples number in the tens of thousands... A small percentage of the passages were obtained from unreleasable texts, so the direct answer version of SciQ is slightly smaller... the quality is not high enough to use them directly without additional filtering by crowd workers.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: we release for future research... SciQ is a useful dataset for studying reading comprehension models in medium-data settings... using SciQ as an additional source of training data improves performance on real 4th and 8th grade exam questions.
